column21:
🧭 Spermatocele/Epididymal Cyst
Benign epididymal-region cystic lesions are common causes of a painless palpable scrotal mass. A spermatocele contains spermatozoa/debris, whereas an epididymal cyst contains simple serous or lymphatic fluid; imaging often cannot definitively separate them, and the distinction is usually clinically minor.
Source Basis: RadPrimer + STATdx master source.

📖 Summary
  • Spermatocele: retention cyst/cystic dilation of the rete testis or epididymal/efferent duct system containing spermatozoa, often with debris; classically in the epididymal head.
  • Epididymal cyst: epithelial-lined epididymal cyst containing simple serous or lymphatic fluid; it may occur anywhere in the epididymis.
  • Best test is grayscale scrotal ultrasound with color Doppler.

🔍 Key Imaging Findings
Ultrasound
  • Simple epididymal cyst: circumscribed, anechoic, thin-walled, avascular cystic lesion.
  • Spermatocele: simple or complex cystic mass, sometimes multiseptated, with internal debris or diffuse low-level echoes due to spermatozoa.
  • Falling snow sign: mobile punctate low-level echoes with Doppler-related acoustic streaming, favoring spermatocele.
  • Dilated rete testis may support spermatocele/efferent-duct obstruction.
  • For a palpable complaint, scan directly over the area of concern.

CT/MRI
  • CT, when encountered, may show a well-circumscribed uni- or multilocular cystic lesion near the superior pole of the testis.
  • MRI: low T1 signal, high T2 signal, and no enhancement; septations may be present.

⚖️ Differential Diagnosis
  • Hydrocele surrounds the testis rather than forming a focal epididymal cyst.
  • Hematocele: trauma context with complex tunica vaginalis fluid containing clot/fibrin strands.
  • Pyocele: epididymoorchitis context with complex tunica vaginalis fluid and often a hyperemic rim.
  • Tunica albuginea cyst: usually small 2-5 mm simple cyst along the testicular surface.
  • Abscess correlates with recent epididymitis and ongoing hyperemia; inguinal hernia changes with Valsalva and shows gut signature or echogenic fat.

🧬 Clinical / Path / Mechanism
  • Etiology is often unknown but may reflect scarring after epididymitis, trauma, or vasectomy; spermatoceles may arise from obstruction/dilation of the efferent ductal system.
  • Reported size range is roughly 3 mm to 10 cm; prevalence is roughly 20-40% of men.
  • Most are asymptomatic or painless palpable masses; rare complications include hypofertility/subfertility or torsion.

📌 Pearls / Pitfalls
  • A cystic extratesticular lesion without vascularized soft tissue is almost always benign.
  • Large lesions may displace the testis and may require a curved-array transducer for complete visualization.
  • Management is usually observation if asymptomatic; spermatocelectomy is reserved for lesions large or symptomatic enough to cause discomfort. RadPrimer notes aspiration/sclerotherapy with 100% alcohol in selected cases.

⭐ Super Summary
  • Think spermatocele when an epididymal-head cyst contains mobile low-level echoes, falling snow, debris, septations, or associated dilated rete testis; accept overlap with simple epididymal cyst when those clues are absent.

🧭 Spermatocele/Epididymal Cyst
Benign epididymal-region cystic lesions are common causes of a painless palpable scrotal mass. A spermatocele contains spermatozoa/debris, whereas an epididymal cyst contains simple serous or lymphatic fluid; imaging often cannot definitively separate them, and the distinction is usually clinically minor.
Source Basis: RadPrimer + STATdx master source.

📖 Summary
  • Spermatocele: retention cyst/cystic dilation of the rete testis or epididymal/efferent duct system containing spermatozoa, often with debris; classically in the epididymal head.
  • Epididymal cyst: epithelial-lined epididymal cyst containing simple serous or lymphatic fluid; it may occur anywhere in the epididymis.
  • Best test is grayscale scrotal ultrasound with color Doppler.

🔍 Key Imaging Findings
Ultrasound
  • Simple epididymal cyst: circumscribed, anechoic, thin-walled, avascular cystic lesion.
  • Spermatocele: simple or complex cystic mass, sometimes multiseptated, with internal debris or diffuse low-level echoes due to spermatozoa.
  • Falling snow sign: mobile punctate low-level echoes with Doppler-related acoustic streaming, favoring spermatocele.
  • Dilated rete testis may support spermatocele/efferent-duct obstruction.
  • For a palpable complaint, scan directly over the area of concern.

CT/MRI
  • CT, when encountered, may show a well-circumscribed uni- or multilocular cystic lesion near the superior pole of the testis.
  • MRI: low T1 signal, high T2 signal, and no enhancement; septations may be present.

⚖️ Differential Diagnosis
  • Hydrocele surrounds the testis rather than forming a focal epididymal cyst.
  • Hematocele: trauma context with complex tunica vaginalis fluid containing clot/fibrin strands.
  • Pyocele: epididymoorchitis context with complex tunica vaginalis fluid and often a hyperemic rim.
  • Tunica albuginea cyst: usually small 2-5 mm simple cyst along the testicular surface.
  • Abscess correlates with recent epididymitis and ongoing hyperemia; inguinal hernia changes with Valsalva and shows gut signature or echogenic fat.

🧬 Clinical / Path / Mechanism
  • Etiology is often unknown but may reflect scarring after epididymitis, trauma, or vasectomy; spermatoceles may arise from obstruction/dilation of the efferent ductal system.
  • Reported size range is roughly 3 mm to 10 cm; prevalence is roughly 20-40% of men.
  • Most are asymptomatic or painless palpable masses; rare complications include hypofertility/subfertility or torsion.

📌 Pearls / Pitfalls
  • A cystic extratesticular lesion without vascularized soft tissue is almost always benign.
  • Large lesions may displace the testis and may require a curved-array transducer for complete visualization.
  • Management is usually observation if asymptomatic; spermatocelectomy is reserved for lesions large or symptomatic enough to cause discomfort. RadPrimer notes aspiration/sclerotherapy with 100% alcohol in selected cases.

⭐ Super Summary
  • Think spermatocele when an epididymal-head cyst contains mobile low-level echoes, falling snow, debris, septations, or associated dilated rete testis; accept overlap with simple epididymal cyst when those clues are absent.

column11: Why can a spermatocele show the falling snow sign on color Doppler ultrasound?
column12: The rete testis and efferent/epididymal ducts normally transport and concentrate sperm. Obstruction or scarring can dilate the ductal system and retain spermatozoa, lymphocytes, and debris within a cystic space. These suspended particles create low-level echoes. Doppler-related acoustic radiation force and acoustic streaming move the particles in real time, producing the falling snow appearance. The mobility of the echoes and absence of vascularized soft tissue favor particulate cyst contents rather than a solid neoplasm.
